title: Why Europe is building both a digital euro and a new mobile payment network
content:
Sending money from your phone seems simple: just choose a contact, enter an amount, and press confirm. But behind these apparently simple actions lie national payment systems that are not always interoperable.

In Europe, the Madrid-based European Network for Payments (ENP) has been established to link five mobile payment solutions operating in 13 European countries: Bizum (Spain), Bancomat (Italy), SIBS-MB WAY (Portugal), Vipps MobilePay (Norway, Denmark, Sweden and Finland) and EPI/Wero (Germany, Belgium, France, the Netherlands, Luxembourg and Austria).

The combined infrastructure of these organisations covers more than 70% of the population of the EU and Norway, serving a total of around 130 million active users.

The ENP’s rollout will be gradual, beginning with payment between individuals before progressing to online shopping and brick-and-mortar businesses.

But as the EU gets ready to launch the digital euro over the next few years, the question that will spring to mind for many is: Why bother?

title: What the US midterms result means for the Ukraine war
content:
The US midterm elections have shifted the balance of power in Congress, delivering a massive blow to Donald Trump and his Republican party. This has implications both at home and possibly abroad, including for US policy towards Ukraine; an issue that was hardly mentioned during the campaigns.

But even if Ukraine did not figure much in the election, the question in US politics of what to do about the war has not gone away. Indeed, in the weeks and months before the result was announced, Trump had been busily rowing back on US support for Ukraine. This was despite much opposition, even from some Republicans.

Crucial intelligence to Kyiv about Russian strikes was cut off, before later being reinstated, while critical military aid was reduced. Trump also decided to suspend several sanctions on Russia.

This move was denounced by President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine as only helping Russia, but justified by Trump as being “in the national interests of the United States” and also a decision that might help his party’s electoral chances by reducing gas prices.

title: Dementia with Lewy bodies: what you should know about the little-known, progressive brain disease
content:
Robin Williams, Monica Vitti, Patrick Stewart or French actress Nathalie Baye: all these famous people lost their lives to dementia with Lewy bodies.

This neurocognitive disease is only tends to get publicity when a celebrity dies from it. Yet it is a common disease (and one of the most common forms of dementia), in France alone it affects about 250,000 people, which makes it the country’s second most widespread neurodegenerative disease, after Alzheimer’s, putting on a par with Parkinson’s. It is estimated that dementia with Lewy bodies (commonly known as “DLB”) affects more than 10 million patients worldwide.

What causes the disease? What symptoms should we look out for? How is it treated? Here is what you need to know.

Dementia with Lewy bodies owes its name to inclusions that develop inside patients’ neurons called “Lewy bodies”, after the German-born doctor Friedrich Heinrich Lewy, who first discovered their existence in 1912.

However, it was only in 1976 that the first clinical case was formally described, while the first international clinical criteria were defined much later in 1996.

title: The Binance hack exploited familiar weaknesses – all organisations should learn from it
content:
Hackers have stolen around US$6.3 billion (£4.7 billion) from the cryptocurrency exchange Binance, most of which was taken in under an hour. According to Binance, the attack exploited systems and individuals with the authority to carry out transactions involving such large sums.

Such vulnerabilities exist everywhere; statistics show that people and the systems they directly use, including their personal computers, remain a top target for cybercriminals. All organisations could therefore learn lessons from this attack.

The Binance theft took place on the evening of October 29, 2026. The Binance attack netted four times the amount stolen in the previous biggest cryptocurrency theft, on the Bybit exchange in February 2025.

Private keys, used to authorise spending or withdrawal from crypto-wallets, are a known vulnerability. But Binance found no evidence these were leaked. An initial statement from the exchange pointed to a compromised laptop belonging to an engineer. This gave the attacker access to the internal system that processes withdrawal requests.

title: Speaking in a second language may shift your moral compass – but it can’t overpower it
content:
In today’s interconnected world, millions of people move between two or more languages every day. They may negotiate at work in one language, speak with family in another, and follow news, entertainment and social media across several others.

Using multiple languages can deeply change the way a person sees the world. Research has suggested that thinking and speaking in different languages can fundamentally shift the way we reason and behave, and even change our morality.

Some studies have suggested that using a second language encourages people to make more rational, utilitarian choices, meaning they prioritise the greatest good for the greatest number of people. This is possibly because moral dilemmas feel less emotionally charged when processed in a second language.

But the effect is not cut and dried – other studies have found little or no such effect.

One reason for these mixed findings is that language is only one part of the story. People do not enter a dilemma as a blank slate – they also bring values, past experiences, and sense of self. To date, most research has focused primarily on which language people use, while paying less attention to the person making the decision.

title: Donald Trump’s Republicans suffer landslide defeat – what this means for the world
content:
Donald Trump’s Republican Party has received a stunning rebuke in the US midterm elections. Republicans went into the evening hoping that the polls might be wrong and that they could at least cling on to control of the Senate. But by midnight in Washington, the GOP was staring down what looked like its worst defeat in 50 years.

Republican losses were not just confined to the type of swing districts that parties usually worry about on election night. The scale of the losses was staggering. They lost Senate seats in deep red states such as Texas and South Carolina. They lost districts they had gerrymandered and in which they were supposed to be unbeatable. They lost seats that even the sharpest analysts thought were safe.

Why? For months, surveys have shown that voters are fed up with high prices, with the war in Iran, and with what is increasingly being talked about as the Trump administration’s corruption. A president who was narrowly elected on the promise of a steady economic hand instead spent two years pursuing an extreme ideological agenda favoured only by a minority of Americans. He ignored what voters were saying, and now they have delivered a harsh verdict.

title: ‘National priority’ policies claim to solve Europe’s housing crisis. They may make it worse
content:
Housing shortages and soaring rents are central to Spain’s upcoming general election. As each party presents voters with ways of addressing the crisis, far right party Vox is backing a simple solution: the principle of prioridad nacional, or “national priority”, which would put Spaniards first in line to receive government benefits.

The policy is central to Vox’s programme. It proposes expanding social housing with priority for Spanish nationals, alongside deregulation and tax reductions.

It is presented as a common sense solution, but national priority does not actually address the root causes of scarcity. In fact, it could even make them worse.

The housing crisis, like many crises, has winners as well as losers: while tenants struggle, landlords collect higher rents and enjoy rising asset values. National priority does not change or tackle these underlying inequalities. Instead, it merely ranks neighbours by entitlement to assistance, while also sowing the seeds of social division.

title: From Wales to Finland, minority language speakers still face prejudice
content:
“How very rude to be speaking Welsh.”

That was the complaint a stranger directed at Patsy, a Welsh learner featured in my latest book, after overhearing her family speaking Welsh in a Cardiff cafe. She could hardly believe it: “But you’re in Wales. What are you talking about?”

Wales has come a long way since the days of the Welsh not, a wooden token often accompanied by corporal punishment that was used in some 19th-century schools to discourage children from speaking Welsh. The Welsh language is now more visible, more widely supported and more politically protected than at any point in history.

But my ongoing research of Welsh-speaking families living in Cardiff suggests that while attitudes have improved dramatically, some linguistic prejudice still lingers beneath the surface. The pattern is not unique to Wales. I found similar experiences among Finland’s Swedish-speaking minority, where official recognition of the language has not always translated into acceptance in everyday life.

title: Canada-EU alliance: as a blueprint for a ‘middle-power bloc’ it has a lot of hurdles to overcome
content:
The dream of a Canada-EU “middle-power bloc” has hit its first serious obstacle. At the Montreal summit, Brussels failed to deliver on the promise of associate membership for Canada, despite the enthusiastic backing of European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen.

Instead, the EU offered the hollow consolation of “an ever-closer association”, raising an uncomfortable question about whether the middle powers can overcome their own divisions to become a serious geopolitical force.

The two-day EU-Canada summit culminated on October 30 with the launch of a so-called “Alliance for the Future”. That compromise formula of association, rather than associate membership – which specifically ruled out full membership – was necessary because of internal disagreements in the EU.

In September, Von der Leyen, offered Canada the chance to become the EU’s first “associate member”. But Germany, backed by Greece and others, objected to the term, worried about legal uncertainty and the expectations it might raise in other countries.

title: Stone-age hunters in northern Europe may have used poison arrows to hunt big prey
content:
Autumn walks in Britain are glorious, as the foliage changes colour and cool crisp air begins to bite. However, some of these European trees hide a much darker secret. For example, the lovely red cup-shaped structures on a yew tree, known as arils, conceal seeds that carry dangerous toxins. These toxins may have been used to poison arrow tips in the past.

A new Danish study has shown that the “smoking gun” is not the poison itself, but the size of the small arrowheads used to deliver the toxin into the hunted animal.

The authors of the latest research examined Danish stone tool technology from the period immediately preceding the arrival of farming in Europe – the Mesolithic.

They argue that the distinctive small size of stone arrow tips from the early Mesolithic period (about 9,000–3,950BC) suggest they were used to hunt large prey with the help of poisons. The poison has long since vanished, leaving only the stone tip.

Arrows that do not use poison are typically larger, since they need to damage the animal’s flesh. But poisoned arrows need only wound a prey animal enough to allow the poison to enter the blood stream.

title: Massive sinkholes open up across Turkey as it struggles with drought and climate change
content:
Turkey’s central Anatolian plateau is one of the country’s most important agricultural regions, producing wheat, maize, sugar beet and other crops. Yet beneath its cultivated fields, the ground is becoming increasingly unstable.

Large sinkholes, some tens of metres wide and deep, have appeared across the Konya basin, swallowing farmland, and threatening nearby roads and settlements.

These collapses can occur suddenly, sometimes in fields that have been cultivated for generations. Around 20 are opening up every year, according to a recent study.

Known locally as obruks, sinkholes are not a new geological phenomenon. They have existed in the Konya basin for thousands of years, but they have become far more frequent over recent decades.

Konya’s sinkholes are consequently both a geological hazard and evidence of a wider water-management problem. The cavities beneath the fields are the product of geological processes extending over thousands of years. Their recent instability, however, is occurring within a groundwater system profoundly altered by human activity and increasingly exposed to drought.

title: How the Sphinx is helping answer a riddle about extinct crocodiles
content:
My colleagues and I discovered a new species of extinct crocodile from a fossil found in the same rocks used to carve the Great Sphinx of Giza.

Today, there are only two species of the long-snouted gavial crocodile, both of which are endangered: Gavialis gangeticus and Tomistoma schlegelii. They are found only in freshwater environments on the Indian subcontinent and Southeast Asia.

However, the fossil record of gavials goes back 80 million years, to the time of the dinosaurs. It shows that they were once diverse, with more than 40 species known, and lived all over the globe. So how did a group of crocodiles that today cannot tolerate saltwater once live all over the world? Our discovery may help to solve this puzzle.

Although the distribution of the continents differed from today, most were already separated by oceans. My colleagues and I have been trying to understand how gavials achieved this cosmopolitan distribution, while also seeking to unlock what led to their current predicament.

title: Spain’s high-speed train network is plagued by old signalling systems. They may have caused the deadly crash
content:
Shortly after 8am, two high-speed trains set off from Madrid’s Atocha station bound for Seville Santa Justa, but neither reached their destination. A failure in the LZB system – an automatic safety, signalling and protection system that monitors trains’ movement and activates automatic emergency braking – triggered a chain of events that led to a fatal accident, which killed 69 people and left many more injured.

Across the EU’s rail network, which spans almost 227,000km, there are more than 25 different, non-interoperable railway signalling systems. These systems (which include the German LZB, the French Crocodile, the Italian BACC and the Spanish ASFA) control and enable the safe movement of trains via blocks, sections of the track that can only have one train on them at any given moment.

On the Andalusia–Madrid line, the German LZB signalling system remains in operation, pending its replacement by the European Rail Traffic Management System (ERTMS) that is already in place on other, more modern lines.

The ERTMS specifications are set out in EU legislation. The aim is for this system to completely replace national ones across the entire EU by 2050.

title: The impossible equation of being a researcher mother, striving to make ends meet
content:
How can we encourage women to pursue scientific careers? In recent years, a number of mentoring or awareness campaigns have been put in place to encourage French high school students to study maths, physics or engineering sciences, while they remain underrepresented in these fields. One of the last large-scale initiatives is the Filles et Maths program, launched in 2025, including work on gender bias, the implementation of “role models” or timetables featuring flexible hours.

The program was nonetheless met with criticism: while women remain under-represented in some disciplines, they also remain a minority in the highest positions across the board in the academic world, from mathematics to social sciences.

In France, gender inequalities are therefore not limited to access to scientific studies: they cut across all university careers and make many women leave French Higher Education and Research before securing tenure. This “drain” is explained by several factors among which motherhood holds an important place. A survey in Denmark illustrates that unlike men, one in three women abandon their scientific career after the birth of their first child.

title: Eurovision 2027: Is Canada singing its way into the European Union?
content:
Officials are meeting this week for the 21st Canada-European Union Leaders’ summit.

It comes only a month after European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen offered Canada associate membership. A draft statement from Montréal, where Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, von der Leyen and EU Council President António Costa met for two days to discuss strengthening ties, calls for an “ever closer association” that will result “in a more active foreign and security policy partnership.”

The talks follow a series of milestones in the relationship between the transatlantic partners, including the announcement in July that Canada was joining the Eurovision song contest. It’s the first country to do so since Australia entered in 2015.

Eurovision is held every year in May, with member countries submitting one original song. Over the years, the event’s format has changed from an exclusive jury vote to a viewer televote and today’s combination of both.

Sometimes, voting can become political, with viewers voting according to their geopolitical preferences or diaspora communities casting ballots for their former home countries regardless of the quality of the performance.
snippet: Officials are meeting this week for the 21st Canada-European Union Leaders’ summit.
creator: Petra Dolata, Associate Professor, History, University of Calgary

title: Barcelona unrest: how to fabricate a protest in the age of TikTok
content:
Imagine coming across a TikTok post calling you to protest for better public schools. You scan a QR code to get more information, and find yourself in a private chat where the instructions are not about education or political organising, but about looting.

This was the picture that emerged in Barcelona on October 24. Around 20 TikTok accounts linked to the anonymous Blocus platform had promoted gatherings across Spain, inviting young people to mobilise.

The public accounts echoed the French student movement and called for similar action in Plaça Catalunya, right next to the city’s housing rights encampment. Yet no evidence links the two movements – a fact that Barcelona’s mayor Jaume Collboni has explicitly acknowledged.

The gathering quickly descended into masked youths smashing shop windows and confronting the police. The night ended with 130 young people arrested, 76 of them underage, and 14 police officers injured.

The TikTok accounts that spurred these particular protests have since been deleted, along with all of their posts and content.

title: Serbia’s leaderless student movement has won a historic election – but what happens next?
content:
Serbia’s leaderless anti-corruption coalition, the Student List, defeated the group led by former president Aleksandar Vučić’s Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) by a comfortable margin in October 25 elections.

Their 53.3% of the vote should get them 141 seats in parliament, well clear of the 125 seats needed to form a majority. The SNS can be a loud but ineffectual opposition with the 103 seats netted by their 39.7% of the vote.

The result was known shortly after polls closed, with Vučić conceding defeat 90 minutes later. Once the celebrations settle down, it looks as if Serbia will manage a peaceful transfer of power to a democratically elected government.

Read more: ‘We changed the system’: how Serbian students ended Alexander Vučić’s 12 years in power

This was not inevitable. By mid-afternoon on election day, news outlets were reporting concentrations of armoured police vehicles and movements of personnel at various spots in central Belgrade.

title: Is France in 2026, Greece in 2009?
content:
France’s ten-year government bond yield reached 5% last week, its highest level in more than two decades. The extra interest it pays over Germany – the “spread” investors use to gauge French-specific risk – has widened dramatically. Parliament is wrestling with a 2027 budget requiring €54 billion in fiscal measures, while protests and violent clashes across France dominate the headlines.

With political instability and social tensions rising, comparisons with Greece at the start of its debt crisis have become inevitable. As Greece’s finance minister when its crisis erupted in 2009, I am increasingly asked how the two situations compare. I understand the temptation, but also how misleading it can be.

France is not Greece. It is one of the world’s largest economies, with globally competitive companies, substantial household savings, a deep financial system, robust institutions. And, unlike Greece in 2009, it has no large external financing imbalance.

title: Warmer seas and shifting pressure systems: the signs that suggest the Mediterranean’s climate is ‘tropicalising’
content:
Nowhere in the Iberian Peninsula or the Balearic Islands has a tropical climate – for this to be the case, the average temperature in the coldest month would have to be 18°C or higher. The contrast between Spain’s winters and summers, and the low temperatures reached in winter, do not resemble those of any tropical climate.

However, over recent decades, climates across Mediterranean basin have begun to show signs of tropicalisation: the process of transitioning towards a tropical climate.

This is evident in several areas, including rising air and sea temperatures, shifting atmospheric patterns, and increasingly erratic rainfall.

Firstly, a marked rise in air temperature – more pronounced than the global average – is making the Mediterranean’s winters shorter and its summers longer, bringing spring forward and delaying the onset of autumn. Some people believe that these transitional seasons have all but disappeared. They do still exist, but they have moved on the calendar.

The temperature of shallow and deep Mediterranean water – down to a depth of around 100m – has also risen markedly.

title: ‘We changed the system’: how Serbian students ended Alexander Vučić’s 12 years in power
content:
Serbia’s student-led political movement has secured a historic election victory. Preliminary results suggest the so-called Student List has won 141 of the 250 seats in parliament, with the ruling Serbian Progressive Party taking 104. The result brings the 12-year rule of Alexander Vučić to an end.

The Student List’s story is remarkable. It has no standalone leader and fielded candidates without political experience from across Serbian society. Stemming from student-led protests against the entrenched corruption and creeping authoritarianism of the ruling regime, it has now achieved an improbable dream.

In late 2025, one of us (Gavin Brent Sullivan) conducted focus groups with members of the student protest movement as part of the Pledge EU Horizon project. The project explores the emotional dynamics of political grievances and their democratic implications.

title: Where did bats come from? New research points to Europe
content:
For decades scientists have argued about where bats originated. A recently published study in the journal Nature offers new evidence to address that question. This new international study combining DNA and fossils supports Europe as bats’ likely birthplace.

The problem thus far has been that, unlike birds, which have a superb fossil record showing the transition from dinosaur to “chicken”, when we find bat fossils, they are exquisitely near-fully formed “bats”.

Bats are the only mammals capable of powered flight. Earlier reconstructions suggested the US, Africa or Asia as bats’ birthplace, with different datasets and models producing different answers. The oldest known bat skeletons, discovered in Wyoming in the US, date to the early Eocene geological epoch, about 52 million years ago. Their elongated wing fingers show that bats could already fly.

However, the location of the oldest known fossils does not necessarily reveal where a group first evolved. These fossils nevertheless provide important clues about early bat anatomy, relationships and distributions. What is missing is a fossil sequence documenting the transition from non-flying ancestors to the earliest flying bats.

title: Lula wins a ‘miracle’ election in Brazil. Now comes the hard part: putting the country back on the right track
content:
Three weeks ago, Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s political obituaries had all been written.

The far-right presidential candidate, Flávio Bolsonaro, son of the jailed former President Jair Bolsonaro, had come out of the first round of the presidential election with a lead that looked impossible to overcome.

At 80 years old, Lula seemed headed for a quiet exit after four decades at the centre of Brazilian political life.

On Sunday, however, Lula proved everyone wrong. He won the runoff and secured a fourth non-consecutive term as Brazil’s president.

The election result is unprecedented in Brazilian politics in at least three ways.

First, no Brazilian presidential candidate had ever won the first round and then lost the runoff. Since the two-round system was adopted by the 1988 Brazilian Constitution, the first-round leader had always gone on to win.

Lula broke that pattern by turning a defeat of around 2.2 million votes in the first round into a solid victory, in three weeks.

title: For Andy Burnham, getting closer to the EU could prove as tricky as exiting it – an expert explains
content:
Andy Burnham has reopened a debate that successive UK prime ministers tried to settle. But the history of Brexit suggests that getting closer to the European Union may prove just as difficult as leaving it.

For years, prime ministers have attempted to put Brexit behind them. Burnham has just done the opposite. By suggesting that Britain could “go all the way” and rejoin the EU, he has broken with the cautious approach of his predecessors.

His intervention has brought renewed urgency to the question: how close should Britain remain to the EU, and on what terms?

The options are not new. From Theresa May’s attempts to secure a bespoke deal to Boris Johnson’s hard Brexit, Rishi Sunak’s pragmatism and Keir Starmer’s reset, governments have grappled with essentially the same dilemma. That is, how can the country retain the benefits of cooperation with the EU without accepting the obligations that come with it?

title: Youth protests across Europe: the overlapping crises facing gen Z
content:
Young people are facing a future that feels increasingly uncertain. Although every generation experiences turbulence while navigating adolescence, the pressures experienced by gen Z – those born between 1997 and 2012 – are different and seem more pervasive.

From climate change and mental health concerns to academic pressure, housing costs, job and economic insecurity, today’s young people are navigating a complex set of expectations. Understanding their frustrations, including those expressed through protests across Europe, requires looking beyond individual experiences to the social conditions shaping their lives.

Adolescence has long been seen as a period of “storm and stress”. This reflecting a belief that is a universal and inevitable period of emotional turmoil, behavioural conflict and identity crisis. However, this has been increasingly challenged.

Rather than being defined solely by difficulty and disruption, adolescence is increasingly viewed as a period of possibility, opportunity and growth. Yet realising that potential depends heavily on the social environments in which young people grow up.

title: From elite spies to ‘gig-economy’ operatives: the changing face of Russian sabotage
content:
Russian hostile activity costs the UK at least £2 billion annually, according to a recent report by Scottish MP Graeme Downie, who has called on the government to measure what these actions cost Britain. But this figure is just the baseline. In reality, a profound shift in Moscow’s approach to sabotage means the true cost is set to climb higher.

While Russia still draws on its cold war target lists, ranging from critical transit nodes and military sites; to energy and communication infrastructure; it has traded highly trained operatives for cheap technology and expendable recruits. The switch to a quantity-over-quality model presents a much more volatile threat.

This model borrows from the logic of distributed computing. It uses networks of cheap, unreliable parts where individual breakdowns are expected yet the overall system still gets the job done.

By generating a high volume of low-cost operations that often fail at the individual level, Moscow still achieves its objectives of causing outsized psychological disruption and steadily exhausting western security services.

title: French students are showing us what protest looks like in the age of viral spectacle
content:
The recent wave of protests in Europe have left us with two striking, viral spectacles of violence and joy. As Limoges’ historic town hall went up in flames, the Orchestre du Nouveau Monde was playing classical music in Paris’ central Place de la République (until the musicians were teargassed by police, that is).

Both scenes offer radically different ways of seeing the protests. The burning town hall offers a powerful image of destruction; the orchestra, of anti-authoritarian collective solidarity. Neither tells the whole story, but their contrast raises important questions: which image will come to represent the protests, and who decides what we see?

France’s demonstrations began with students protesting deteriorating school conditions, including staff shortages and dilapidated buildings. But they quickly intersected with broader anger over living costs and public services.

The unrest also formed part of a wider European moment. On the same weekend, people took to the streets in Spain, Italy, Belgium, Portugal and Albania. Grievances include low wages, rising energy prices and unaffordable housing, each within its own national context.

title: France’s ‘casseurs’: why the term fails to do justice to the extent of looting and spiralling unrest
content:
Following widespread looting sprees and acts of violence occurring on the sidelines of the October 17 student protests, so-called “casseurs” seem to be the centre of attention. But the term, which comes from the French verb casser or “to break”, poses more questions than answers. The sociologist Paolo Stuppia examines the unprecedented situation many cities across France are having to contend with, and the complex combination of collective action whose motivations are unclear and the social media’s extreme agility.

The Conversation: How unprecedented are the scenes of looting that we witnessed on the sidelines of the October 17 demonstrations?

Paolo Stuppia: What may be unprecedented is the extent of the destruction of private property and the goods that have been stolen. It should be clear, however, that not all the looters can necessarily be sorted into identifiable groups, at least politically.

title: Elderly women are often victims of gender-based violence. Why is it so hard for them to get help?
content:
In 1997, Ana Orantes appeared on an Andalusian television programme to recount a lifetime of abuse at the hands of her husband. Just a few days after her harrowing testimony, she was brutally murdered by her abuser. Her case prompted a widespread reckoning on gender-based violence in Spain, which led to significant legislative reforms.

Ana Orantes died at the age of 60 as an elderly woman who had suffered violence and abuse for 40 years. But today, despite the impact that her case had, older victims of gender-based violence remain marginalised, to the point of being practically invisible. They do not fit the social stereotype of a victim, which we tend to associate with a young woman, often with young children in her care.

But while gender-based violence affects all kinds of women, of all ages and from all walks of life, not all victims find themselves in the same circumstances. And for any intervention to work, it must take this complex reality into account.

Elder gender-based abuse often merges two realities: domestic violence stretching back years or decades, and abuse of older people associated with dependence and care, often in the form of neglect or psychological abuse.

title: New long-clawed British dinosaur is the first of its kind in Europe
content:
The fossilised skull of a new species of mysterious meat-eating dinosaur from the Isle of Wight has been rediscovered in the collections of the Natural History Museum after over 100 years in storage.

Over its nearly 150-year history, this London museum has become home to over 30 million specimens, making it fairly easy to forget about the odd fossil or rock here and there. This is almost definitely what happened to the only known fossil of the UK’s newest dinosaur, a two-legged meat-eating theropod (the dinosaur family including birds) which we have named Invictibellatrix amberina in a new study.

title: Is it better to vaccinate against COVID and flu together, or separately?
content:
As autumn sets in and temperatures fall across the northern hemisphere, vaccination campaigns are getting underway. Vaccination is not just the most effective way to prevent severe forms of infection and avoid hospital admissions – it also protects health systems, preventing them from becoming overburdened when annual case numbers reach their peak.

The viruses that cause flu and COVID are constantly evolving, meaning we gradually lose any immunity we have acquired over time. The vaccines used in each campaign are therefore specifically formulated and adapted each year, in response to the most recent variants identified by the World Health Organization’s global surveillance and monitoring networks.

Contrary to popular belief, the primary aim of vaccination programmes is not to prevent infection. Instead, they aim to reduce the severity of the disease, the risk of hospitalisation, admission to intensive care units, and deaths among those at higher risk of complications.

title: The mafia isn’t keeping fentanyl out of Europe – the lack of demand is
content:
Fentanyl and other synthetic opioids are still the single biggest driver of overdose deaths in the US. They were involved in around 38,000 of the roughly 70,000 deaths recorded in 2025, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

Europe’s figures are of a different order. In 16 countries that reported data, fentanyl and its derivatives were linked to a total of around 210 drug-induced deaths in 2024, up from about 130 in 2023. Most of that rise may involve medicines rather than illicitly made fentanyl.

Other potent synthetic opioids, notably nitazenes, have driven recent peaks in deaths in several countries. In Italy, the government’s latest report on addiction counted only five fentanyl-related deaths in 2025.

This gap has prompted a striking explanation: that Italy’s mafias, wary of a drug that kills their customers and draws police attention, have chosen to keep fentanyl out.

It is a compelling story. But it does not fit what we know about drug markets or mafias. Europe’s comparatively low fentanyl numbers are better explained by something less cinematic: there is very little demand for it.

title: The little-known 14th century battle that has shaped English, Scottish and French relations
content:
On October 17, 1346, the battle of Neville’s Cross was fought outside Durham in the north-east of England. It was a decisive moment in Anglo-Scottish history that led to the capture of King David II of Scotland. Yet few have heard of it.

Other battles are far better known. Those of Stirling Bridge (1297), Falkirk (1298) and Bannockburn (1314) are more famous because of the exploits of William Wallace and Robert the Bruce. Similarly well-known are the successes of Edward III, the Black Prince and Henry V at Crécy (1346), Poitiers (1356) and Agincourt (1415), respectively.

Yet, less than two months after Crécy, a decisive victory was won in northern England. The battle of Neville’s Cross remains one of the least publicly known but decisive battles in English history.

As Edward III gathered a force of 15,000 men to invade France in 1346, King Philip VI of France requested Scottish aid. He wrote to King David in June and again in July: “I implore you to remember our friendship and our treaties and to strike as hard at England as you can.”

With Edward III and most of his nobles in France, Philip reassured David that England was a “defenceless void”. The opportunity was too good to miss.

title: Maricarmen Abascal: how a disabled, evicted 87-year-old woman became a political football in Spain’s upcoming election
content:
In Spain, an average of 44 evictions are carried out every day. While statistics like this are shocking, numbers alone rarely spark a revolution. Mass protest movements instead tend to rally around one compelling individual story.

This was exactly what happened with 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal, who has become so famous that she is known in Spain as simply Maricarmen. Following an insurmountable rent hike and a lengthy legal battle, she was evicted from her Madrid home of 71 years in September, and died on October 7. She quickly become a household name, and the figurehead of Spain’s housing protests.

Her case stirred the empathy of millions, and inspired collective shame that society was unable to prevent an elderly woman from being forced out of her home on a stretcher. Her story made headlines around the world, sparked a wave of fierce, nationwide protests, and led to an unravelling of Spanish politics that has culminated in a snap election on November 29 and a general strike planned for November 11.

title: How one of the world’s biggest music stars is transforming the Spanish language
content:
According to the Royal Spanish Academy (RAE, under its Spanish acronym), a “piquete” is either a sharp object, a small wound, or a group of striking workers blocking access to a workplace. It is a word, generally speaking, of conflict and harm.

But when Puerto Rican musician Benito Antonio Martínez Ocasio – more commonly known as Bad Bunny – intones on his song NUEVAYoL “Tú tiene’ piquete mami, yo también” (“You’ve got piquete mami, and so do I”), he is not talking about trade unions or pointy sticks. He is referring to something else altogether, a way of moving through the world with a certain self confidence, attitude and style.

In Puerto Rico’s boricua dialect, the meaning of piquete is totally divorced from the RAE’s official uses. But unapologetic use of his native dialect is what defines the music of the world’s biggest Spanish-language musician.

Bad Bunny has put Spanish on more global stages than any other artist in recent history, yet he is also widely criticised for his way of speaking. This is rife on social media, where users complain that he “doesn’t talk properly”, he is “deforming the language”, and “doesn’t enunciate clearly”.

title: French school protests: a rite of passage – and the result of genuine concerns
content:
Across France, school students have taken to the streets to protest about teacher shortages, dilapidated school buildings and long school days.

While the tradition of student protest has long roots in France, the country’s current fiscal crisis combined with entrenched structural problems with teacher recruitment, sickness absence and a backlog of school maintenance means this is unlikely to be something the current government can easily address.

Problems – and protests – regarding conditions in French schools go back decades.

I’ve spent 20 years conducting research in France and protest has been a recurring theme. Many research participants I’ve worked with have spoken with fondness about protesting as high school students.

One participant in Nanterre, who went on to become a community activist, repeatedly spoke about how schools in poor Paris suburbs were institutions that would “crush you”. This was due in part to French educational culture, but also because of their under-resourcing and poor state of repair. To them protest felt like an outlet for these grievances.

title: How the ‘geopolitical stigma’ associated with Putin’s Russia is affecting ordinary Russians
content:
Russia’s international standing collapsed within weeks of its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Sanctions swept across Russian banks, businesses and political elites, while western companies exited the country en masse. For those living inside Russia, it was the everyday, tangible shifts that made this feel real.

Western goods disappeared from supermarket shelves, direct flights to Europe stopped and getting visas to travel abroad became more difficult. Russian athletes, artists and scholars, meanwhile, were excluded from international competitions, cultural platforms and academic events.

For Russians living elsewhere in Europe, the change was often more subtle. Questions about their nationality in job applications, negative media coverage and offhand comments about Russia all contributed to a growing sense that being Russian now meant carrying a stigma. Russia’s changing international reputation had suddenly become personal.

title: Inside two prison systems: why Denmark and the UK punish so differently
content:
It has been said that a society should be judged not by how it treats its outstanding citizens but by how it treats people who break the law.

I research prisons and am interested in what incarceration reveals about the relationship between the state and the people in its care.

By this standard, the UK and Denmark tell very different stories. In 2025, Denmark’s prison population stood at around 69 people per 100,000 residents, compared with about 170 per 100,000 in the UK – roughly one and a half times higher.

One way to understand this difference is through welfare. With its wide range of universal welfare state services such as heavily subsidised daycare, free healthcare, free education and high standards of public services, Denmark’s criminal justice system has traditionally placed greater emphasis on rehabilitation and reintegration. Prisoners retain the right to vote, maintain closer contact with family and are generally encouraged to participate in ordinary social life where possible.

title: China and the EU could turn Morocco into a surprise global hub for electric vehicles
content:
China now makes more than seven in ten of the world’s electric cars. In 2024 it produced over 12 million, 1.25 million of which were exported, mainly to Europe.

The EU is worried about this – alarmed by cheap, state-subsidised Chinese vehicles flooding its market and threatening the 13 million jobs which depend on its own auto industry. So the bloc has spent the past two years building a system of tariffs and rules to keep Chinese cars at bay.

In 2024, it imposed extra duties of up to 35% on Chinese electric vehicles (EVs), on top of an existing 10% import tariff. So far though, the EU’s tactics have yielded limited results.

Chinese vehicle sales in Europe nearly doubled between 2024 and 2025.

And much of this sales volume is being driven by the EV powerhouse that is developing at speed in Morocco.

Chinese firms producing cars in Morocco avoid exposure to those EU tariffs, and have announced US$6 billion (£4.5 billion) of investment in battery and electric car component plants in the country.
